plinys-two-ministrae

The two women belonged to the Scattered Households, the house churches of Antioch, Asia Minor and Rome. Their story shows these churches from the outside, and it shows women holding an office early enough for a Roman governor to know its name. Third-Century Anatolia is the region's church about 130 years later.
Card: Pliny records them as ministrae, the first office-holders in Asia Minor attested by a hostile witness. Census: Scattered Households tells their story.
abitinian-martyrs

The Abitinians are where Donatism's story begins. Their bishop had handed over the Scriptures, and they reportedly refused communion with him. That refusal grew into the Donatist conviction that a sacrament is only as valid as the purity of the one who gives it. Latin Pastoral is the church of Cyprian and Augustine, which faced a rival Donatist church in the same towns.

Card: the break with the bishop, hedged. Census, Donatism: 'A sacrament's validity rises and falls on the giver's own unbroken purity.' Census, Latin Pastoral: 'A rival Donatist church stood in the same towns.'
benjamin-lay-burlington
Lay is where Quaker opposition to slavery starts, as one man's protest. A generation later John Woolman made it the Quakers' own position, and Woolman owned and read Lay's book.
Card: the protests, the book, Philadelphia Yearly Meeting moving toward barring slaveholders. Census, Quakers: Woolman's journal and traveling 'turned Friends against slaveholding'.
le-chambon-sur-lignon

The plateau's Protestants were heirs of the Huguenots and the Church of the Desert, and the villagers themselves trace their rescue to the memory of worship in hiding. Their story shows a persecuted church's past turned, generations later, into shelter for others. The Confessing Church stood against the Nazi state in Germany in the same years; the two had no organizational link.
Card: 'kept a memory of the persecutions of the Desert'; the villagers' own reason. Old line: no organizational link.
asad-shidyaq

The American missionaries in Beirut called As'ad their first convert and first martyr, so his story stands at the start of the Arab Evangelical churches. It also shows how the first meeting between Protestant missions and the Eastern churches was remembered: as martyrdom by one side, as discipline by the other. The Maronite church held him at Qannubin, its patriarchal monastery, where he died.
Census, Arab Evangelicals: Jessup calls him 'the first convert and the proto-martyr'. Card caveat: 'the Maronite documents ... read the same events as discipline'.
hungarian-galley-pastors

This episode belongs to Hungary's Protestants, whose churches lost pastors to the galleys in these years. Its closest parallel is the Huguenot galley convicts of the same generation, in the Church of the Desert. The survivors' release shows how far Protestant Europe's network reached: their letters found readers in four countries, and the Dutch, heirs of the Dutch Reformation, sent a fleet.
Card: letters reached Dutch, Swiss, German and English Protestants; the States General instructed de Ruyter. Census, Hungary Protestants: 'Some pastors went to the galleys'.
hrotsvitha-of-gandersheim

The map has no Ottonian German tradition, so the links here are neighbors in time. Her plays show that tenth-century learning did not live only in the reformed monasteries. The Benedictine Reform of Late Anglo-Saxon England and Cluny were its contemporaries, but Gandersheim was a house of secular canonesses, outside that reform.
Card: canonesses of Gandersheim, the plays. Old line: secular canonesses, not a reformed Benedictine convent. The middle sentence is a reading of those two facts.
nickel-mines-forgiveness

The Amish are a branch of the Anabaptist family, which began with adult baptisms at Zurich in 1525 and split again in the 1690s. Their response shows how deep that family's teaching runs. Scholars trace it to the Lord's Prayer said every day and to a memory of martyrdom reaching back to the Radical Reformation. Their later history is told with the Mennonites.
Card: scholars trace the response to the daily Lord's Prayer and 'a communal memory of martyrdom reaching back to the Radical Reformation'. Census: Anabaptists, Zurich 1525; Mennonites & Amish.
